To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the number of training examples, the invariances afforded to the agent's frame of reference, and the variety of visual inputs available to the agent all affect the generalisation of a neural network; (2) these findings suggest that the propensity of networks to generalise systematically can be increased by increasing the variety of observations that they receive during learning, as in human children.
the number of object-word experiences in the training data and the visual invariance afforded by the agent’s frame of reference make a difference to the performance of the agent.

the degree to which neural networks generalise in systematic, human-like ways depends on the number of object experiences in the training data set, the invariances afforded to the network by the agent's frame of reference and the richness of the agent's perceptual input.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding the environmental drivers of systematicity in a neural network-based cognitive architecture.
understanding how the environment can influence the way in which a network learns to generalise.
the extent to which the performance of neural networks on tasks of generalisation is sensitive to the particulars of the training regime or environment in which the task is instantiated.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the degree of out-of-sample performance that neural networks exhibit is dependent upon a variety of factors that include the number of experiences that the network has been exposed to, and the nature of the environment that it has been trained within.
the degree to which a network generalizes depends on the particulars of the environment.
the degree to which neural networks generalise depends on the environment and the training regime.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the generalisation ability of a deep neural network depends on the training data and the environment in which it is tested.
the generalization of neural networks is not just a matter of the architecture and training procedure, but it also depends on the environmental context of the learning process.

the degree of out-of-sample systematicity and generalisation that networks display can depend critically on the particulars of the environment and training regime in which a given learning task is instantiated.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the environment in which learning is situated is an important factor in determining the extent to which neural networks generalise beyond the immediate experience of training.
we need to consider the environment in which an agent is situated when evaluating its generalisation performance.
the environment in which learning occurs can play a critical role in the degree of out-of-sample systematicity that is exhibited.
